mixing-001.question: A liquid with density 1200 kg/m³ and viscosity 1.0 Pa·s is stirred at 120 rpm with an impeller 0.30 m in diameter. Which combination of the impeller Reynolds number Re = ρND²/μ and flow regime is correct? As a guide, take the regime as laminar if Re is below about 10 and turbulent if above about 10⁴.
choices: About 220, transitional
About 720, transitional
About 1.3×10⁴, turbulent
mixing-001.explanation: Converting the speed to revolutions per second, N = 120/60 = 2.0 s⁻¹, and Re = 1200 × 2.0 × 0.30²/1.0 = 216, about 220, in the transitional regime. About 1.3×10⁴ uses the speed of 120 in rpm, and because the units are inconsistent it wrongly indicates turbulence. About 720 does not square the impeller diameter, using ρND/μ, a combination that is not dimensionless. The impeller Reynolds number uses ND as the characteristic velocity and the impeller diameter as the characteristic length, so its regime boundaries also differ from those of pipe flow Re = ρuD/μ. In the transitional regime the power number changes with Re, so power is found by reading the Np–Re curve.

mixing-002.question: The shaft torque of an agitator was measured as 5.0 N·m at 300 rpm. Approximately what is the agitation power (friction losses in bearings and the like have been subtracted)?
choices: 9.4 kW
mixing-002.explanation: Shaft power is P = 2πNT, with N in revolutions per second. Since 300 rpm = 5.0 s⁻¹, P = 2π × 5.0 × 5.0 = 157 W. Taking the product of the angular velocity ω = 2πN = 31.4 rad/s and the torque gives the same result. 9.4 kW uses the speed of 300 in rpm and is 60 times too large. 25 W forgets the 2π and simply multiplies revolutions per second by torque. Dividing the power found from torque by ρN³D⁵ gives the power number, the basis for comparing impeller performance. Note that power derived from the motor's electrical input includes losses in the motor and gearbox and comes out somewhat high.

mixing-003.question: Which is correct about the relationship between the power number Np = P/(ρN³D⁵) and the impeller Reynolds number Re in a baffled stirred tank?
choices: In the laminar regime Np is nearly constant and power is proportional to density; in the turbulent regime Np is inversely proportional to Re and power is proportional to viscosity
Np is determined only by the impeller shape and is constant regardless of Re in every regime

In the laminar regime Np is inversely proportional to Re and power is proportional to viscosity (P ∝ μN²D³); in the turbulent regime Np is nearly constant and power does not depend on viscosity (P ∝ ρN³D⁵)
mixing-003.explanation: In the laminar regime viscous forces dominate and Np·Re is constant, so P = (constant) × μN²D³: power is proportional to viscosity and independent of density. In the turbulent regime inertial forces dominate, and in a baffled tank Np is nearly constant (about 5 for a Rushton turbine), so power is proportional to density and independent of viscosity. The explanation that swaps the laminar and turbulent relations is wrong. Np depends not only on the impeller shape but also on the presence of baffles and on Re, so saying it is constant in every regime is also wrong. In an unbaffled tank, Np keeps falling even in the turbulent regime as swirl strengthens. Design uses the Np–Re curve for each impeller.

mixing-004.question: In a baffled tank, a Rushton turbine (power number Np = 5.0, constant in the turbulent regime) with a diameter of 0.20 m is run at 3.0 s⁻¹ to stir water (density 1000 kg/m³). Approximately what is the agitation power?
choices: 1.1 kW
mixing-004.explanation: Turbulent power is P = NpρN³D⁵, so P = 5.0 × 1000 × 3.0³ × 0.20⁵ = 5.0 × 1000 × 27 × 0.00032 = 43.2 W, about 43 W. Taking the viscosity of water as 1.0 mPa·s, Re = 1000 × 3.0 × 0.20²/0.001 = 1.2×10⁵, in the turbulent regime where Np can be taken as constant. 1.1 kW is the 1080 W obtained by cubing the impeller diameter, and 14 W is the 14.4 W obtained by squaring the speed. Power is proportional to the fifth power of impeller diameter, so doubling the diameter needs 32 times the power at the same speed. The impeller diameter has a very large effect on power, so Re and Np are checked before the motor size is decided.

mixing-005.question: A low-viscosity liquid such as water was stirred by an impeller rotating at high speed at the center of a cylindrical tank without baffles. Which correctly describes what tends to happen and the effect of baffles?
choices: Swirl strengthens mixing, so adding baffles makes mixing worse and also lowers the power number
No vortex forms in low-viscosity liquids, and baffles are needed only when stirring viscous liquids in the laminar regime

The whole liquid swirls with the impeller and a vortex forms at the center; top-to-bottom mixing is weak and air is easily entrained. Fitting baffles to the wall turns the swirl into axial and radial flow and also increases the power number
mixing-005.explanation: In a tank without baffles, the liquid rotates with the impeller as swirling flow, and a vortex forms with the center of the surface depressed. The relative velocity between impeller and liquid becomes small, so power is hard to put in, top-to-bottom mixing is weak, and at higher speeds the vortex reaches the impeller, entraining air and causing vibration. Fitting four baffles about 1/10 to 1/12 of the tank diameter wide to the wall turns the swirl into axial and radial flow, and the turbulent power number becomes a nearly constant, large value. Saying swirl strengthens mixing is backward. In the laminar regime of viscous liquids swirl hardly develops and baffles instead create stagnant zones, so it is in the turbulent regime of low-viscosity liquids that they are needed.

mixing-006.question: A polymer solution with a viscosity of about 100 Pa·s is to be mixed uniformly throughout the tank. Which choice of impeller is most appropriate?
choices: Run a Rushton turbine of small diameter at high speed
Use a helical ribbon impeller (or an anchor), whose large diameter close to the tank diameter sweeps the whole tank at low speed
Run a small-diameter propeller at high speed to create a strong axial discharge flow
mixing-006.explanation: A viscous liquid falls in the laminar regime with a small impeller Reynolds number, where the impeller can move liquid only very close to its blades and flow does not carry far. Running a small impeller at high speed mixes only its surroundings, leaving motionless regions near the wall and surface. Close-clearance impellers with a diameter of 0.9 or more of the tank diameter, which sweep the entire tank, are therefore used: a helical ribbon creates top-to-bottom circulation, and an anchor renews the liquid at the wall and aids heat transfer. A Rushton turbine creates strong radial discharge and shear and suits gas–liquid dispersion in low-viscosity liquids. A propeller is an axial-flow impeller suited to circulating low-viscosity liquids and suspending solids, and its flow does not carry in viscous liquids.

mixing-007.question: In a stirred tank holding 1.6 m³ of liquid, an impeller with a flow number Nq = Q/(ND³) of 0.75 (diameter 0.50 m) is run at 2.0 s⁻¹. Approximately how long does it take for the tank contents to pass once through the impeller discharge flow Q (the circulation time V/Q)?
mixing-007.explanation: The discharge flow is Q = NqND³ = 0.75 × 2.0 × 0.50³ = 0.1875 m³/s, and the circulation time is V/Q = 1.6/0.1875 = 8.5 s. 4.3 s squares the impeller diameter, overestimating Q as 0.375 m³/s, and 6.4 s forgets to multiply by the flow number, taking Q = ND³. Impeller diameter enters the discharge flow to the third power because the flow velocity is proportional to ND and the discharge area to D². The liquid has to circulate several times before the tank becomes uniform, and the mixing time is often several times the circulation time, so the circulation time is a guide for estimating how fast mixing is. Note that the total circulating flow, including liquid entrained by the discharge, is larger than Q.

mixing-008.question: In a baffled stirred tank operating in the turbulent regime, the mixing time θm is to be halved. If only the rotational speed is changed, with the same tank and impeller, by approximately what factor does the agitation power change? Take N·θm and the power number as nearly constant in the turbulent regime.
choices: 8 times
2 times
4 times
mixing-008.explanation: If N·θm is constant, θm ∝ 1/N, so halving the mixing time requires doubling the speed. If the power number is constant in the turbulent regime, P ∝ N³, so the power becomes 2³ = 8 times. 2 times assumes power is proportional to speed, and 4 times assumes it is proportional to the square. The energy used for one mixing operation, P·θm, also increases in proportion to N², by 4 times, so speeding up mixing by raising the speed is costly. Other measures, such as switching to a larger impeller or feeding near the impeller, are considered as well. Note that N·θm can be taken as constant only in the turbulent regime; in the transitional and laminar regimes N·θm increases as Re decreases.

mixing-009.question: A stirred tank operating in the turbulent regime is scaled up with geometric similarity. Which is correct about the similarity rule that keeps the impeller Reynolds number the same as in the small tank (with the same liquid)?
choices: It gives the same result as constant power per unit volume P/V, so dispersion and mass transfer can also be matched

The rotational speed falls in inverse proportion to the square of the impeller diameter, and P/V falls in inverse proportion to the fourth power of the diameter, so agitation in the large tank becomes extremely weak and the rule is hardly ever used in practice
Since the speed need not change, the mixing time can also be kept the same as in the small tank
mixing-009.explanation: Keeping Re = ρND²/μ constant with the same liquid requires N ∝ D⁻², and substituting into the turbulent P/V ∝ N³D² gives P/V ∝ D⁻⁴. Doubling the impeller diameter makes the speed 1/4 and P/V 1/16, and agitation becomes extremely weak. Constant P/V is a different similarity rule giving N ∝ D^(−2/3), and the results are not the same. Constant speed is the rule that matches mixing time, and with it P/V grows in proportion to D². In the turbulent regime Np is nearly constant regardless of Re, so there is little need to match Re itself, and the similarity rule is chosen to match the quantity that governs the process result, such as solid suspension, bubble dispersion, shear or mixing time.

mixing-010.question: The minimum rotational speed needed to suspend particles that have settled on the bottom of a stirred tank, until no particle remains on the bottom for more than 1–2 seconds, is called the just-suspended speed Njs. In the same tank, with all other conditions unchanged, which single change increases Njs (makes the particles harder to suspend)?
choices: Changing to particles with a larger density difference from the liquid
Changing to particles of smaller diameter
Replacing the impeller with one of larger diameter
mixing-010.explanation: In Zwietering's correlation, Njs ∝ ν^0.1 dp^0.2 (gΔρ/ρL)^0.45 X^0.13 D^(−0.85), so the larger the density difference Δρ, the more readily particles settle and the larger Njs becomes. Reducing the particle diameter dp lowers Njs, though with an exponent of 0.2 the effect is relatively weak. Enlarging the impeller diameter D strengthens the flow at the bottom at the same speed, so Njs falls. Impeller type and clearance from the bottom also have a large effect, and a down-pumping axial impeller placed near the bottom can suspend particles with less power than a Rushton turbine. Above Njs, solid–liquid mass transfer improves little, so agitation for dissolution or reaction is economically run only slightly above Njs.

mixing-011.question: A solid–liquid suspension tank is scaled up with geometric similarity, doubling the impeller diameter. If the just-suspended speed follows Njs ∝ D^(−0.85) (with the same particles and liquid) and the power number is constant in the turbulent regime (P ∝ N³D⁵, V ∝ D³), by what factor does the power per unit volume P/V needed for complete suspension change?
choices: About 0.50 times
About 0.68 times
1 time (no change)
mixing-011.explanation: The speed becomes 2^(−0.85) ≈ 0.555 times. Substituting into P/V ∝ N³D² gives P/V ∝ D^(3×(−0.85)+2) = D^(−0.55), or 2^(−0.55) ≈ 0.68 times. 1 time is the value for scale-up by the constant-P/V rule, which overestimates the power if suspension is the only aim. About 0.50 times is the value for constant tip speed (N ∝ 1/D), where the speed of 0.5 times falls below the Njs ratio of 0.555, so particles remain on the bottom of the large tank. The total power, proportional to D^2.45, becomes about 5.5 times. Reported exponents of D for Njs differ by study, from about −0.67 to −0.85, and −2/3 would be the same as constant P/V, so actual scale-up is confirmed by small-scale tests.

mixing-012.question: Air is blown (sparged) from below a Rushton turbine stirring water. If the gas flow rate is increased at constant rotational speed, which correctly describes the change in agitation power?
choices: Bubbles resist the flow, so the power rises above the ungassed value
Power is determined only by the liquid density and impeller shape, so it does not change with gas flow rate
Gas collects behind the blades to form gas cavities, weakening the force with which the blades push the liquid, so the power falls below the ungassed value
mixing-012.explanation: When gas is introduced, it gathers in the low-pressure region behind the blades to form gas cavities, reducing the drag on the blades, so the power falls at the same speed. For a Rushton turbine at high gas rates, the gassed power Pg can fall to about 40–60% of the ungassed value. The bubbles also lower the mean density of the dispersion. Saying bubbles resist flow and raise the power is backward, and saying it does not depend on gas rate overlooks the cavity effect. The motor is chosen to withstand the ungassed power in case aeration stops, and kLa correlations use the gassed Pg/V. Impellers with concave blades show a smaller drop in power.

mixing-013.question: In an aerated stirred tank, if the speed is too low for the gas flow, the impeller becomes blanketed with gas and cannot disperse bubbles, and the gas rises around the shaft as large bubbles (impeller flooding). Which operation is appropriate to eliminate this condition?
choices: Raise the speed or reduce the gas flow
Lower the speed further so as not to break up the bubbles
Remove the baffles to make the liquid swirl and gather the bubbles at the center of the tank
mixing-013.explanation: The amount of gas an impeller can disperse depends on its pumping capacity ND³, and flooding occurs when the gas flow number Qg/(ND³) exceeds a limit. The limiting gas flow number increases with the Froude number N²D/g, so raising the speed or reducing the gas flow returns the tank to complete dispersion, in which the impeller breaks up the bubbles and spreads them throughout the tank. Lowering the speed reduces the dispersing capacity further and makes flooding worse. Removing the baffles makes gas gather at the center with the swirl, and together with the surface vortex, dispersion actually gets worse. The basic practice is to feed gas from a ring sparger smaller than the impeller diameter directly below the impeller so the gas is reliably drawn into it.

mixing-014.question: A fast reaction A + B → R (the desired product) is carried out by gradually adding liquid feed A to feed B in a stirred tank. R further reacts with A to form the by-product S (R + A → S). The reactions proceed faster than mixing, and S is to be reduced. Which method of feeding A is most appropriate?
choices: Drip it from above the liquid surface near the wall, where the flow is slow
Add it all at once in a short time, since the result does not depend on the feed location
Add it slowly through a feed pipe inserted into the liquid near the impeller, where turbulence is intense and the discharge flow is fast
mixing-014.explanation: When reaction is faster than mixing, a region rich in A remains around the feed point, where R that has formed meets excess A and becomes S. Feeding into a place with a high energy dissipation rate, such as the impeller discharge, mixes A in quickly and finely, and adding it slowly also suppresses local excess of A. Near the wall at the surface, turbulence is weak and A stays concentrated for a long time, increasing S. Adding it all at once makes A excess throughout the tank, the least favorable option. In such mixing-sensitive reactions, selectivity changes with feed location, feed rate and speed, and the yield can fall when the mixing time lengthens on scale-up, so particular care is needed in scale-up.

mixing-015.question: When a pseudoplastic (shear-thinning) fluid such as an aqueous xanthan gum solution is stirred with a small impeller, a region that moves only around the impeller (a cavern) can form, with the liquid outside it remaining almost stationary. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Near the impeller, where the shear rate is large, the apparent viscosity falls and the fluid flows easily, but away from the impeller the shear rate is small and the apparent viscosity is large
The shear rate increases with distance from the impeller, lowering the apparent viscosity and stopping the flow
Pseudoplastic fluids have the property that viscosity increases with time under continued stirring (rheopexy)
mixing-015.explanation: The apparent viscosity of a pseudoplastic fluid decreases as the shear rate increases. The shear rate is large near the impeller, can be taken as proportional to the speed on average (about 10 to 13 times N in the Metzner–Otto method), and becomes smaller toward the wall. So although the liquid near the impeller flows well, viscosity rises with distance and the flow weakens, and in liquids with a yield stress the outer region stops. Saying the shear rate increases with distance from the impeller reverses the distribution. Rheopexy, in which viscosity increases with time, is a time-dependent property distinct from shear thinning. Remedies include impellers of larger diameter, close-clearance impellers or multiple impellers, or raising the speed to extend the cavern to the tank wall.
